newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cypriots eye U.N. talks with wary optimism.
newsitem.headline: Cypriots eye U.N. talks with wary optimism.

text.p: Cypriots were in a mood of subdued optimism on Wednesday as their leaders prepared to meet in New York for U.N.-backed talks on resuming negotiations to end the division of their island.

Disappointed many times in the past, Cypriots were reluctant to display much optimism at what may come out of the first encounter between President Glafcos Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash in nearly three years.
"I am happy to see the talks starting as a first step but I don't expect a solution in the short term," said Turkish Cypriot businessman Salih Celiker, 43.

In Nicosia, Cyprus's capital divided by a "Green Line", teenage soldiers barely out of school still lurk in watchtowers stacked with sandbags and festooned with rival flags sprouting on a skyline of minarets, deserted buildings and churches.

Celiker lives in northern Cyprus, the breakaway Turkish Cypriot state declared in 1983 nine years after mainland Turkish forces seized the territory in response to a brief Greek Cypriot coup in Nicosia inspired by the military ruling Greece.

"I want to see a solution in which the presence, identity and sovereignty of the Turkish Cypriots is accepted," he added, expressing a common fear among the Turkish Cypriot community of domination by the larger Greek Cypriot community.

Meanwhile disillusioned Greek Cypriots living in the south are hoping that U.S. pressure on Turkey --- particularly that of presidential emissary Richard Holbrooke -- can push the peace process forward.
"Something might happen," shrugged Andreas Kyriakou, a 35-year-old businessman whose family lost their home during the Turkish invasion.

"The Americans are involved this time so they might be able to twist Turkey's arm. But," he added with a touch of sarcasm, "(Bulent) Ecevit is back in the (Turkish) government and we all know what that means. He thinks he solved the Cyprus problem in 1974."
Ecevit, now deputy prime minister in Mesut Yilmaz's government, ordered the Turkish invasion of Cyprus in 1974 when he was prime minister.

Greeks and Turks have been estranged since the outbreak of intercommunal violence in 1963 which prompted the dispatch of a U.N. peacekeeping force a year later -- now the longest serving in the world.

The talks are just the latest attempt by the international community to reunite the island under a federal umbrella -- a solution agreed in principle by the two sides in 1977 and 1979 but with key disagreements outstanding on the mechanisms of implementing it.

The stalemate has nurtured hostility and suspicion between the two sides, climaxing last year in a series of deaths during clashes along the "Green Line" slicing through the island manned by U.N. peacekeepers.
Each side is beefing up its defences and the conflict remains an open sore in relations between NATO partners Greece and Turkey.

The Greek Cypriots, whose administration is internationally recognised as the government of Cyprus, are due to take delivery of anti-air missiles from Russia next year if a solution is not found in the meantime. Ankara has vowed to block their deployment.
But some Cypriots said an accord on Wednesday between Greece and Turkey at a NATO summit in Madrid promising to settle disputes by peaceful means could help the New York talks.
"They are two separate issues, but an improvement in the climate between Greece and Turkey should have an effect here as well," said Greek Cypriot accountant Marios Pavlou, 29.
On the other side of the divide, 31 year-old-lawyer Latif Aran expressed similar sentiments.

"I am hopeful for the upcoming New York talks because of the conciliation reached by Turkish and Greek officials yesterday in Madrid. I do not expect any immediate solution from the New York talks for the Cyprus question but I hope they will be the start of solution process."
